624.title: The nine reminders
624.hook: Marcus lists nine things to recall when offended: we're made for each other, they act from beliefs, we err too (Meditations 11.18)
624.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations copy out the nine reminders and reread them when someone has offended them, often before replying.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Phocion. Your line was theirs, and mine. Who got your kindness, and what did they do with it? Day six hundred twenty-four.

Someone offends you, and the old script starts running: how dare they, who do they think they are, wait till I tell everyone. Marcus wrote a different script. It's a long entry, and it's numbered, first, second, third, like a checklist a pilot runs before takeoff, item by item. He wrote it to read when someone offended him, a list to run before the reply goes out. Today: my child.
screen: `HOW DARE THEY.` → `A NUMBERED CHECKLIST.` → `THE NINE REMINDERS.`

segments.voice: First, about them. One: we're made for one another. Two: think what these people are like at the table, in bed, and what beliefs are driving them. Three: if they're right, don't complain; if they're wrong, it's unwillingly, out of ignorance. No soul, Marcus says, is willingly cut off from the truth. Second, about you. Four: you do plenty of wrong yourself, and even when you don't, you have the tendency, held back only by fear or concern for your reputation. Five: you don't even know for certain that they're doing wrong; many things are done for reasons you can't see. Six: when you're furious, remember that life is a moment, and soon we'll all be laid out. Third, about the anger. Seven: it isn't their acts that disturb us; those live in them. It's our own judgments. Take away the judgment that it's terrible, and the anger goes with it. Eight: our anger and grief hurt us more than the things that caused them. Fourth, the last. Nine: kindness is invincible, if it's real, not a fake smile or an act. What can the most violent person do if you stay kind, and at the very moment they try to harm you, gently say: no, my child, we were made for something else; you won't harm me, you're harming yourself, my child. Then Marcus adds a tenth, as a gift, he says, from the leader of the Muses: to expect bad people not to do wrong is madness.
screen: `ONE TO THREE: KIN, BELIEFS, IGNORANCE.` · `FOUR TO SIX: ME TOO, UNSURE, BRIEF.` · `SEVEN AND EIGHT: MY JUDGMENT, MY ANGER.` · `NINE: KINDNESS IS INVINCIBLE.` · then, large: `NINE REMINDERS.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring to mind one person who offended you recently. Now, slowly, run the nine. We're made for each other. They act from their beliefs. If they're wrong, it's unwilling. I've done the same. I can't be sure. Life is short. It's my judgment that hurts. My anger hurts more. Kindness can't be beaten. Let each one land for a breath, and notice which one loosens the knot. The bell holds the time.
My child. Marcus's gentle answer to real harm: no, my child, we were made for something else; you're only harming yourself. Today's word.
Your line: nine reminders. Next time someone offends you, run even three of them before you answer. Day six hundred twenty-four.

625.title: Four failures
625.hook: the mind fails four ways: false impressions, unsocial acts, false words, letting the body rule (Meditations 11.19)
625.howItsDone: Stoic readers sometimes use Marcus's four checks as a quick daily review: needless thoughts, divisive acts, insincere words, and moments when appetite took over.

segments.voice: Yesterday: my child. Your line was nine reminders. Which reminder loosened a knot for you? Day six hundred twenty-five.

Mechanics have a short list of the ways an engine goes wrong. Doctors have one for the body. Marcus, right after his nine reminders, wrote a short list of the ways a mind goes wrong: four of them, each with a sentence to say when you catch it. It reads like a small diagnostic card, the kind you could tape inside a kitchen cabinet and glance at every morning. Today: four failures.
screen: `AN ENGINE'S SHORT LIST.` → `THE MIND'S SHORT LIST.` → `FOUR FAILURES.`

segments.voice: First, the frame. There are four wrong turns of the ruling part of the mind, Marcus writes, that you should constantly watch for, and wipe out when you catch them, saying a line to each. Second, the first two. One: a thought you don't need. When you catch it, say: this thought isn't necessary. The replay of an old argument, a worry you've already dealt with, a fantasy that goes nowhere. Two: something that pulls people apart. Say: this loosens the bonds between people. A cutting remark, a bit of gossip, a scheme that works for you by working against others. Third, words. Three: you're about to say something that isn't what you really think. Marcus says to count it among the most absurd things there are, to speak not from your own mind. Flattery, a fake agreement, a performance. Fourth, the body. Four: the moment you catch yourself reproaching yourself, because the more divine part of you has been beaten and has given way to the less honorable, mortal part, the body and its coarse pleasures. Notice what he calls it: a defeat of the ruling part, not a crime. So four questions, really. Is this thought necessary? Does this act bind people or break them? Do I mean what I'm about to say? Who's in charge here, my reason or my appetite? He doesn't ask himself never to fail. He asks himself to catch it, wipe it out, and keep going.
screen: `FOUR WRONG TURNS TO WATCH FOR.` · `UNNEEDED THOUGHTS, UNSOCIAL ACTS.` · `WORDS YOU DON'T MEAN.` · `APPETITE IN CHARGE.` · then, large: `FOUR FAILURES.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last day. Check for one of the four. An unneeded thought that kept looping. A word or act that pulled people apart. Something you said that you didn't mean. A moment your appetite ran the show. Don't scold yourself; just find one. Name it with Marcus's line: this isn't necessary, or this loosens the bonds, or this isn't my real mind. Then let it go. The bell holds the time.
Four failures. Marcus's short list of the mind's wrong turns: needless thoughts, unsocial acts, words you don't mean, and appetite in charge. Today's word.
Your line: wipe it out. Run the list once today, catch one failure, name it, and wipe it out. Day six hundred twenty-five.

626.title: Remember a good person
626.hook: keep someone who lived virtuously in mind (Meditations 11.26)
626.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations keep a particular person in mind, a grandparent, a teacher or a figure from history, and in hard moments ask what that person would do.

segments.voice: Yesterday: four failures. Your line was wipe it out. Which one did you catch, and did you wipe it out? Day six hundred twenty-six.

A voice can turn up just before a corner gets cut. A grandmother's, a coach's, a teacher who believed in someone. That person might not have been seen in years. They might not be alive. But in certain moments they're right there, and it's easier to stand a little straighter. Marcus had an old rule for exactly that. He'd found it written down somewhere, and copied it into book eleven. Today: Ephesians.
screen: `THE VOICE AT THE CORNER.` → `STANDING A LITTLE STRAIGHTER.` → `REMEMBER A GOOD PERSON.`

segments.voice: First, the rule. In the writings of the Ephesians, Marcus says, there was this precept: keep constantly in mind one of the people of the past who lived with virtue. That's the whole entry. Second, a puzzle about the source. Who were these Ephesians? Nobody is sure. Some editors have suggested it should read Epicureans, followers of Epicurus, and there's a reason to think so. Seneca, in his eleventh letter, passes on Epicurus's advice: choose some good person and keep them always before your eyes, living as if they were watching. Either way, Marcus says plainly that the rule wasn't his own; he copied it. Third, Marcus did it himself. Book one of the Meditations reads like this practice. It's a list of people and what he learned from each: his grandfather's good temper, his mother's generosity and simple way of living, his teachers, his adoptive father Antoninus. Before the hard thinking begins, Marcus stops to remember good people, one by one, and what each gave him. Fourth, why it works. A rule is abstract. A person is concrete. In a hard moment, what's right? is a big question. What would she do? often answers itself. The person you remember doesn't have to have been perfect. They only have to be good in the one way you need right now.
screen: `KEEP A GOOD PERSON IN MIND.` · `EPHESIANS, OR EPICUREANS?` · `BOOK ONE IS THIS PRACTICE.` · `WHAT WOULD SHE DO?` · then, large: `REMEMBER THEM.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Bring one good person to mind: living or gone, famous or known only to you. See their face. Hear their voice. Remember one specific thing they did, one moment that showed who they were: the words they used, where you were standing. If gratitude comes, let it. Then picture a moment coming up today when you'll need them, and imagine them there with you. The bell holds the time.
Ephesians. The source Marcus names for his rule to keep a good person in mind, though some editors think it should read Epicureans. Today's word.
Your line: remember them. At one hard moment today, ask what your good person would do. Day six hundred twenty-six.

screen: `DAY 626 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NO THIEF OF THE WILL.`

627.title: No thief of the will
627.hook: Marcus quotes Epictetus: no one can rob us of our will (Meditations 11.36)
627.howItsDone: Readers of Epictetus and Marcus often respond to a loss by naming what remains in their control, their response, and making one deliberate choice about it.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Ephesians. Your line was remember them. Whose face did you call up, and when? Day six hundred twenty-seven.

Someone steals your bike. Someone takes credit for your idea. Someone cuts your hours, or your budget, or your part in the school play. Life has a lot of thieves. Toward the end of book eleven, Marcus stops writing his own thoughts for a while and copies out a string of sayings from Epictetus, the teacher who had once been enslaved. One of them is only a few words long, and it names the one thing no thief can take. Today: Epictetus.
screen: `LIFE HAS A LOT OF THIEVES.` → `MARCUS COPIES EPICTETUS.` → `NO THIEF OF THE WILL.`

segments.voice: First, who's speaking. Epictetus was born into slavery, studied philosophy, and later taught it as a free man in Greece. As far as we know, Marcus never met him. But in book one Marcus thanks his teacher Rusticus for lending him Epictetus's discourses from his own library. Near the end of book eleven, Marcus writes out several Epictetus lines in a row, like favorite quotations copied into a notebook. Second, the line. A thief of the will, Marcus quotes, doesn't exist. No one can rob you of your choice. Third, the word. The Greek is prohairesis: the power to choose, to decide what you'll agree to, what you'll want, what you'll do. For Epictetus it's the one thing that truly belongs to you. Your body, your possessions, your reputation, your job can all be taken. Your choice about how to meet the loss can't be. Fourth, what it doesn't mean. It doesn't mean nothing hurts, or that circumstances don't matter. A person in prison has fewer choices than a person on a beach, and Epictetus knew that better than most. But even inside narrow walls, he taught, there's still the choice of how you stand there. That small, steady choice is what no one can steal.
screen: `EPICTETUS, ONCE ENSLAVED.` · `NO ONE CAN ROB YOUR CHOICE.` · `PROHAIRESIS: THE POWER TO CHOOSE.` · `EVEN INSIDE NARROW WALLS.` · then, large: `NO THIEF.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of something that's been taken from you, small or large: time, a plan, an opportunity, a person's trust. Let yourself feel the loss honestly. Then look for what wasn't taken: your choice about how to respond, right now. Pick one small choice you'll make about it today: a word, an action, an attitude. Hold it. Nobody handed it to you, and nobody can take it. That one is yours. The bell holds the time.
Epictetus. Born into slavery, he taught that a thief of the will doesn't exist, and Marcus copied his line into book eleven. Today's word.
Your line: no thief. When something is taken from you today, name the choice that's still yours, and make it. Day six hundred twenty-seven.

screen: `DAY 627 COUNTS.` → `TOMORROW: NOW, IF YOU WANT IT.`

628.title: Now, if you want it
628.hook: all you pray to reach later, you can have now, if you stop refusing it (Meditations 12.1)
628.howItsDone: Readers who take this entry to heart often notice when they're postponing a good life until conditions change, and look for the part of it that's available today.

segments.voice: Yesterday: Epictetus. Your line was no thief. What choice did you make that no one could take? Day six hundred twenty-eight.

Someday, when the kids are grown. Someday, when the debt is paid off. Someday, after the promotion, after the move, after the test results come back clear. Then I'll be calm. Then I'll be kind. Then I'll really live. Book twelve is the last book of the Meditations, and its very first entry starts by taking apart that word, someday. Today, as the last book begins: now, if you want it.
screen: `SOMEDAY, WHEN.` → `THEN I'LL REALLY LIVE.` → `THE LAST BOOK OPENS.`

segments.voice: First, the claim. All the things you hope to reach by a long, roundabout road, Marcus writes, you can have now, if you don't refuse them to yourself. Second, how. Three moves. Leave the past alone. Hand the future over to providence. And set the present right, just the present, toward reverence and justice. Third, what those two words mean here. Reverence, he says, so that you love what has been given you, since nature brought it to you, and you to it. Justice, so that you speak the truth freely and plainly, and act according to law and to what each thing deserves. And don't let anything stop you: not other people's badness, not their opinions, not your own body's complaints. Fourth, the sting at the end. Then Marcus writes the line that makes this entry worth carrying. It isn't death you should fear, he says, but never beginning to live according to nature. A lot of our somedays are a way of postponing the beginning. Near the end of his notebook, Marcus says the beginning has been available all along. Not after the next promotion, the next move, the next quiet season. Now, if you stop refusing it. The life he's describing isn't waiting at the end of the road. It's at your feet.
screen: `WHAT YOU SEEK, YOU CAN HAVE NOW.` · `LEAVE THE PAST, TRUST THE FUTURE.` · `SET THE PRESENT RIGHT.` · `FEAR NEVER BEGINNING.` · then, large: `NOW, NOT LATER.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Look for one good thing that's already here: the chair holding you, the breath moving, a person in the next room, a quiet minute, a meal waiting. Something you usually postpone enjoying until later, until you've earned it. Let yourself have it now. Don't save it. Don't earn it first. Just receive it, fully, for this one minute, as if it were enough. The bell holds the time.
Now. Marcus opens his last book: everything you hope to reach by a long road, you can have now, if you stop refusing it. Today's word.
Your line: now, not later. When you hear yourself say someday today, ask what part of it you could have now. Day six hundred twenty-eight.

629.title: Their opinion, strangely
629.hook: we love ourselves most but trust others' opinion of us more than our own (Meditations 12.4)
629.howItsDone: People who draw on this passage sometimes pause before seeking reassurance and first ask what they themselves honestly think, then act on it when it's reasonable and kind.

segments.voice: Yesterday: now, if you want it. Your line was now, not later. What did you stop postponing? Day six hundred twenty-nine.

You've decided the outfit looks good. Then someone glances at it a certain way, and suddenly it doesn't. You were sure the idea was solid, until a coworker raised one eyebrow. It's odd. We spend every waking minute with ourselves, know our own reasons better than anyone, and still hand the verdict to whoever happens to be looking. Marcus noticed the same oddness, and wrote it down as a puzzle. Today: their opinion, strangely.
screen: `THE OUTFIT, AND THE GLANCE.` → `ONE RAISED EYEBROW.` → `THEIR OPINION, STRANGELY.`

segments.voice: First, the puzzle. I've often wondered, Marcus writes, how it is that every person loves himself more than anyone else, and yet sets less value on his own opinion of himself than on other people's opinion of him. Second, the test. Then he proposes a thought experiment. Suppose a god, or a wise teacher, stood beside you and told you never to think anything you wouldn't say out loud the moment you thought it. Nobody could bear it, he says, not even for a single day. Third, what that shows. So we're more concerned with what our neighbors will think of us than with what we think of ourselves. We guard the outside carefully and leave the inside to anyone. We'll rewrite an email five times for how it sounds, and let a mean thought run all morning unchecked. Fourth, turning it around. Marcus isn't saying other people's views never matter; a friend's honest criticism can be a gift. He's pointing at a strange imbalance. The one person who's with you every minute, who knows your reasons and your efforts, gets the smallest vote. Today's practice gives that person, you, a little more say: look honestly, decide, and let your own judgment stand without checking the room first.
screen: `LOVE OURSELVES, TRUST THEM MORE.` · `SAY EVERY THOUGHT ALOUD?` · `WE GUARD THE OUTSIDE.` · `GIVE YOURSELF A VOTE.` · then, large: `MY OWN OPINION.`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Think of a choice you've been second-guessing because of what someone might think: a plan, a purchase, the way you dress, a thing you want to say. Set their imagined opinion aside for a moment. Ask yourself honestly: what do I think? Is it reasonable? Is it kind? If the answer is yes, decide to trust it, just this once, without asking anyone to approve it first. Notice how that feels, and stay with it. The bell holds the time.
Their opinion. Marcus's puzzle: we love ourselves most, yet value other people's opinion of us more than our own. Today's word.
Your line: my own opinion. Make one decision today on your own honest judgment, and don't check the room before you act. Day six hundred twenty-nine.

630.title: What will you be?
630.hook: consider what you'll be when death arrives (Meditations 12.7)
630.howItsDone: Some readers of the Meditations keep a few written words describing the person they hope to become, and reread them as a way of sorting what matters in an ordinary day.

segments.voice: Yesterday: their opinion, strangely. Your line was my own opinion. Where did you trust your own judgment? Day six hundred thirty, the end of a week.

People write wills about what they'll leave behind: the house, the savings, the watch for the grandson. A will rarely says who you hope to be by then. Marcus comes at that second question near the very end of his notebook, in a single sentence. He doesn't ask what you'll own when death comes. He doesn't ask what you'll have achieved. He asks something harder. Today: vast gulf.
screen: `A WILL FOR WHAT YOU LEAVE.` → `NOT FOR WHO YOU ARE.` → `WHAT WILL YOU BE?`

segments.voice: First, the sentence. Consider, Marcus writes, what condition you ought to be in, body and soul, when death overtakes you. Then think about how short life is, the vast gulf of time behind and ahead of it, and how fragile all matter is. Second, the shape of it. Notice the order. First the person. Then the timeline: a short life set inside an enormous stretch of time. Then the material: everything made of stuff that breaks down. He isn't trying to frighten himself. He's trying to see clearly, so that what matters stands out. Third, why be and not have. Death will find you somewhere, doing something. Marcus doesn't ask where. He asks what kind of person it will find. That moves the question from achievements to character. You can't control when; you can work on who. Fourth, the week, looking back. Nine reminders. Four failures. Remember them. No thief. Now, not later. My own opinion. And now, what will I be. Each one was a way of shaping the person death would find: someone who answers offense with reasons, catches the mind's wrong turns, remembers good people, keeps hold of the choice, begins now, and trusts their own honest judgment. Book twelve is drawing the notebook toward its close, and this is the question it hands you.
screen: `WHAT SHOULD DEATH FIND?` · `SHORT LIFE, VAST TIME, FRAIL MATTER.` · `BE, NOT HAVE.` · `A WEEK OF SHAPING A PERSON.` · then, large: `WHAT WILL I BE?`

segments.voice: Settle, and breathe. Imagine, gently, a day many years from now. Who would you like to be by then? Not what you'd like to have. Who. Kind? Patient? Honest? Brave? Let two or three words come. After the bell, if you like, write them somewhere you'll see them: a note on your phone, a scrap of paper in your wallet. For now, just hold the words, and breathe. The bell holds the time.
Vast gulf. Marcus sets a short life against the vast gulf of time behind and ahead of it, and asks what you'll be when death comes. Today's word.
Your line: what will I be. Write down two or three words for who you want to be, and do one thing today that fits them. Day six hundred thirty.
